title: Rocks and soil

accuracy.evidence: Checked on 25 Nov 2026 against the National Curriculum in England Year 3 Rocks programme of study ('recognise that soils are made from rocks and organic matter'); USDA NRCS soil texture classes (sand 0.05-2 mm, silt 0.002-0.05 mm, clay under 0.002 mm), quoted on the shake-test buttons; the USDA NRCS teaching figure for a typical loam (about 45% mineral, 5% organic matter, 25% water, 25% air by volume), drawn as the bar chart in step 1; FAO (2015) International Year of Soils ('up to 1,000 years to produce 1 cm of soil'); and RHS guidance on sandy, clay and loam soils (sand drains fast and dries out, clay holds water, can waterlog and bakes hard, loam suits most plants). The 80, 50 and 15 ml drain figures are labelled in the adult text as a demonstration in the real order, not measured values. Worms mix humus in; the lesson says they do not eat rock.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented primary misconceptions about soil (Happs 1984, Journal of Geography; Science Learning Hub 'Alternative conceptions about soil': soil seen as inert, uniform and unchanging): soil is just crushed rock or just dirt (step 1 prediction, the 'rock' slip, the Ella mastery item); the tiniest bits sink first (step 2 prediction, wrong-order feedback naming grain size); smooth clay must drain fastest (step 3 prediction, the 'drain' slip, cylinders showing 15 ml); sand or clay is best for every plant (step 4 feedback and the 'job' slip); soil forms in a few years and worms make it by eating rock (step 5 order feedback and the 'time' slip).

lab_distinct.evidence: The mechanism is a soil-science bench: a jar that accepts only soil's real parts and then shows the loam bar chart, a settling simulation where sand, silt and clay layers drop in turn after a shake and must be named bottom first, three funnels draining 100 ml into graduated cylinders over a simulated minute, a job card dragged onto grainy sandy, loam and clay bins, and a cross-section that cracks, crumbles, gains humus and a worm as the formation steps are ordered. It is not flagrock (digging to bedrock), flagrocktype (igneous, sedimentary, metamorphic), flagerode (erosion) or flagcups (capacity); the lab_distinct gate measured under 30% source overlap with every flag_*.js.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each idea is found before it is stated: plastic and sugar bounce out of the jar with a reason, and the loam chart appears only once the five parts are in; after the shake the jar shows the sand layer forming first, so 'big bits sink first' is seen; the cylinders fill to visibly different heights before the child is asked which soil let most through, and the follow-up asks which held most, turning the same reading into water-holding; in step 5 the cross-section only gains soil once cracking and breaking come before rotting and mixing.

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions, each with a tempting wrong option that the lab disproves: 'Is soil just crushed rock?' (yes, only crushed rock); 'After a shake, which bits sink to the bottom first?' (the tiniest clay bits, the common intuition that small things fall first); 'Which soil lets water through fastest?' (clay, because it is smooth). Tasks cannot complete until the prediction is locked, and the done message names the child's own prediction.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Eight challenge questions; every wrong option carries a tagged slip with its own message: 'rock' (soil is rock bits mixed with humus, water, air and life), 'settle' (big sand sinks first, clay last), 'float' (humus floats, sand sinks), 'drain' (big gaps between sand grains, tiny gaps in clay), 'job' (pure sand dries out, pure clay waterlogs, loam suits vegetables), 'time' (weathering is slow, up to 1,000 years per cm).

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use short sentences, name each science word once and explain it in the same sentence (humus, silt, loam), and validate_lessons.py passed the family readability limits. Lab banners are one or two short sentences, cards are 1 to 7 words with a picture, and particle sizes on the shake buttons give the precise curriculum detail without needing it to play.

no_filler.evidence: Each kid paragraph teaches one idea (what soil is made of; particle sizes and settling; drainage and the three soils; how slowly soil forms). The adult paragraphs give the curriculum statement and key words, the sourced numbers and which figures are a demonstration, the named mistakes, and what each lab step does. The content gate found no filler phrases and under 12% overlap with any other lesson.

mobile.evidence: Checked on iPhone 13 screenshots in dark and light themes and desktop in light for every step: the jar and loam chart sit side by side above a 4-column card grid (64 px+ tall), the settled jar's layer labels sit to its right, the shake buttons wrap to a 2 by 2 grid, the three funnels and cylinders with ml readings fit at 390 px, soil bins and job pictures fit in three columns, and the formation cards stack one per row. After a fix the loam bar labels sit above the bars, so nothing is clipped at the canvas edge.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a button twin with a descriptive aria-label ('Put humus in the jar', 'Shake the jar', 'Next layer up: Silt', 'Choose Sandy soil', 'A veg patch for most plants: Loam soil', 'Next step: Rain, ice and roots crack the rock'), so dragging is optional. The canvas aria-label updates with every result, challenge feedback is a polite live region, the fig carries the young class for larger tap targets, and walk.cjs ran axe WCAG 2.1 AA in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13.

FAO (2015) International Year of Soils fact sheets: soil formation
Royal Horticultural Society, Soil types (sandy, clay, loam)
